report.source_text: CT with contrast showed a hypervascular 3.4 x 4.7 x 6.1 cm mass that extended from the nasal cavity to the oropharynx (Figures 2A-2F). The left maxillary sinus demonstrated erosion of the medial wall, making it the likely site of origin. Posterior maxillary sinus bowing (Holman-Miller sign) was not noted and the pterygopalatine fossa and pterygomaxillary fissure were not widened, making JNA less likely. All of the paranasal sinuses demonstrated mixed attenuation accumulation of fluid except for the right frontal and right superior ethmoidal sinuses, likely reactive. Left-sided cervical lymphadenopathy was also noted.

report.source_text: MRI of the face and neck revealed a large, heterogeneously enhancing polypoid mass that appeared to arise from the left nasal mucosa or left maxillary sinus and extend into the nasopharynx and oropharynx (Figures 3A-3D). Abnormal signal enhancement involved the left pterygopalatine fossa, and the mass was noted to extend into the left mastication space. The left maxillary sinus medial wall appeared eroded, which may be secondary to vascular invasion or chronic inflammatory processes. Sinonasal carcinoma or rhabdomyosarcoma was favored based on the radiological findings.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Angiomatous inflammatory nasal polyp with no malignancy identified.
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 16-year-old male presented with a six-month history of epistaxis, nasal obstruction, foul-smelling nasal discharge, and weight loss. Physical examination revealed bilateral polyposis and a soft palate mass. CT and MRI imaging showed a large, hypervascular mass extending from the nasal cavity to the oropharynx, with erosion of the left maxillary sinus medial wall and left-sided cervical lymphadenopathy. While imaging raised suspicion for malignancy (sinonasal carcinoma or rhabdomyosarcoma), Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) was considered less likely. Initial biopsies of the mass showed granulation tissue and necrotic tissue with bacteria, but no malignancy. An arteriogram confirmed the hypervascularity of the lesion, showing a tumor blush from the left internal maxillary artery, and the polyp was successfully embolized. The known final diagnosis of an angiomatous inflammatory nasal polyp with no malignancy was ultimately established.

Initial biopsies of the mass showed granulation tissue and necrotic tissue with bacteria, with no malignancy identified.
